title: What finance is
objective: Name the three areas of finance (personal, corporate, markets) and why money decisions compound over a lifetime

q.prompt: Mia puts aside **$10 a week** from age 25 to 65 and never touches it. Guess: how much has she put away? (Ignore interest for now.)
q.explanation: $10 × 52 weeks × 40 years = $20,800. A tiny weekly habit becomes a big number because it repeats for decades.

q.prompt: Which of these is a **finance** question?

options.text: Should I keep my savings in a bank or pay down my car loan?
Which train gets me to work fastest?
options.why: That's about time and transport, not managing money.

options.text: What's the best way to cook rice?
options.why: Cooking isn't finance, even if rice is cheap!

q.explanation: Finance is about how money is earned, saved, borrowed, invested and spent, and the choices between them.

q.prompt: True or false: $1,000 earning 5% interest a year grows by exactly $50 every year.
q.explanation: Year 1 adds $50. Year 2 adds 5% of $1,050, which is $52.50. You earn interest on your interest, so growth speeds up.

screens.title: Finance has three big areas
screens.body: **Personal finance** is your money: pay, spending, saving, debt, tax and [[super]]. **Corporate finance** is how businesses raise and spend money. **Financial markets** are where money is traded, like the [[ASX]]. This course starts with you, then works outwards.

screens.title: Money decisions compound
screens.body: A choice you repeat every week is really thousands of choices. And money left to grow earns returns on its past returns. That's [[compounding]]: small, early, steady decisions end up mattering more than big, late ones.

visual.label: after 2 years at 5% a year: the extra $2.50 is interest on interest

screens.title: Worked example: Jack's coffee
screens.body: Jack buys a $5 coffee every day. Is that a problem? Finance doesn't judge; it just makes the trade-off visible.

lines: The question isn't 'is coffee bad?' but 'is it worth that to me?'

q.prompt: Match each decision to its area of finance.
pairs: A company borrowing to build a factory
Shares changing price on the ASX
q.hint: Ask: whose money is it, and where is the decision made: a household, a business, or a market?
q.explanation: Super is your money (personal). A firm's funding is corporate. Prices set by buyers and sellers are markets.

q.prompt: Priya spends $15 a week on food delivery fees. How much is that over a year (52 weeks)?
q.explanation: $15 × 52 = $780 a year. Seeing the yearly total makes it easier to decide if it's worth it.

q.prompt: $1,000 earns 5% a year and you leave the interest in. What is it worth after 2 years?
q.hint: After year 1 it's $1,050. Now add 5% of $1,050.
q.explanation: $1,050 + 5% of $1,050 ($52.50) = $1,102.50. The second year earns more because the balance is bigger.

q.sentence: Working out your own pay, bills and savings is called ___ finance.
q.explanation: Personal finance covers your own money decisions, which is where this course begins.

q.prompt: Sam cancels a $12-a-month streaming service he never watches. How much does he keep over 5 years?
q.explanation: $12 × 12 months × 5 years = $720, from one five-minute decision.

q.prompt: Two friends save the same amount each year at the same interest rate. Ana starts at 25, Ben at 35. Both stop at 65. Who ends up with more?

options.text: Ana, because her money has ten extra years to compound
They end up about the same
options.why: Ana's money grows for longer, and growth builds on growth.

options.text: Ben, because he saves when he earns more
options.why: Here they save the same amount, so only time differs, and time favours Ana.

q.explanation: Ana saves for 40 years, Ben for 30, and Ana's early savings also earn interest on interest for longer.

q.prompt: Sort each one: is it about your own money, or about businesses and markets?

items.text: A fund manager trading shares on the ASX

q.explanation: Cards and holiday savings are household decisions; share issues and trading belong to companies and markets.

screens.title: Your turn
screens.body: Pick one small thing you pay for every week. Multiply it by 52. Is the yearly number worth it to you? No right answer; just notice it.
screens.action: Find one weekly spend and work out its **yearly cost**.

bullets: Finance has three areas: personal, corporate and markets.
Small repeated choices add up to big yearly and lifetime totals.
Interest earns interest, so starting early beats starting big.

reviewBank.prompt: A business deciding whether to borrow money for a new warehouse is an example of…

options.why: It's the business's money, not a household's.
Markets are where things are traded; this is a company's own funding choice.

reviewBank.explanation: How a business raises and spends money is corporate finance.

reviewBank.prompt: A $4 snack every workday (5 days a week, 48 working weeks). What's the yearly total?
With compound interest, the dollar amount of interest you earn each year gets bigger over time (if the rate stays the same).
reviewBank.explanation: Each year's interest is calculated on a larger balance, so it grows.

reviewBank.prompt: Starting to save ten years earlier usually matters more than saving a little more each year later.
reviewBank.explanation: Extra years give compounding more time to work, which often beats bigger but later contributions.
